cim: The Proper Use of Artificial Intelligence in Writing
cim_eredeti: The Proper Use of Artificial Intelligence in Writing
szoveg_eredeti:
There is a great deal of discussion today about artificial intelligence and its role in writing. Some people speak of AI-generated copy as if it is the end of human authorship. Others treat AI as just another productivity tool, no different from spellcheck, transcription software, or a digital thesaurus. As a publisher and editor in chief for nearly 50 years, I believe the truth sits somewhere in the middle.

Writing has never been a purely solitary act. As far back as I can remember, generating strong, meaningful, and publishable copy has always been a team effort. I have been blessed throughout my career to work with some of the best copywriters, proofreaders, researchers, editors, designers, and thinkers in the business. They have helped me sharpen ideas, refine language, challenge assumptions, verify facts, and present work in a way that meets the highest editorial standards.

That does not make the work less mine. It makes the work better.

In any creative process, the team matters. The best editorial teams understand the writer's voice. They know the mission. They know the audience. They know when to adjust a phrase, when to strengthen an argument, when to ask for more evidence, and when to leave the language alone. Their role is not to replace the author. Their role is to help the author achieve the purpose of the work.

That is how I view artificial intelligence.

AI, when used properly, is simply another member of the editorial team. It can help organize thoughts, clean up a rough draft, suggest structure, identify gaps, assist with research, and improve clarity. It can help a writer move from a dictated thought to a readable message. It can help an editor test whether an article flows, whether a headline works, or whether a paragraph needs more precision.

But AI should not be mistaken for the author.

My belief is simple: if the concept starts with you, if the outline is yours, if the thesis is yours, and if the final judgment is yours, then using an editorial team that includes AI is fair game. The human being must remain present at the beginning and at the end of the process. The human being must provide the intent, the values, the point of view, and the accountability.

What is not acceptable is allowing AI to generate creative or editorial copy from beginning to end without clearly labeling that work as AI-generated. When there is no human author shaping the idea at the beginning, no human editor reviewing the result at the end, and no transparency about the role AI played, then we have crossed an important line.

If I dictate an email into an AI tool and ask it to format, organize, and polish the message before I send it, that is an acceptable use. The thought is mine. The intent is mine. The final approval is mine. AI is helping me present my message more clearly.

But if an email comes to me and an AI agent responds on my behalf without my knowledge, judgment, or review, that is something different. It may be practical in some settings, but it is not the same as a human-generated response. At minimum, we need to be clear about when a person is speaking and when a system is speaking for them.

The same principle applies to article writing.

If you write the draft, create the outline, develop the thesis, and then use AI to help format the piece, strengthen the structure, support the research, or fill in gaps, that is an acceptable and responsible use. In that case, AI is functioning like an editor, researcher, or production assistant.

But if you simply give AI a theme, tell it how many words to write, and allow it to create the article from beginning to end, then that work should not be presented as though it came fully from a human writer. It may be useful. It may even be well written. But it lacks the human origin, lived experience, editorial accountability, and authentic voice that readers have a right to expect.

This is where publishers, editors, educators, and communicators must be thoughtful. We do not need to reject AI. We do need to define its role.

AI can be a powerful assistant. It can help us work faster. It can help us reach more people. It can help us preserve ideas, organize knowledge, and support writers who may struggle with structure or mechanics. It can help transform spoken ideas into written communication. It can help an editor see options that may not have been obvious in the first draft.

But AI must serve the mission, not replace it.

For those of us who have spent decades building platforms of trust, this distinction matters. Readers trust that a publication has standards. They trust that editors are making decisions. They trust that stories are being shaped by people who understand context, culture, history, and consequence. That trust cannot be handed over blindly to a machine.

The proper use of AI in writing requires three commitments: authorship, transparency, and accountability.

Authorship means the idea begins with a human being. The writer brings the purpose, the voice, the experience, and the judgment.

Transparency means we are honest about the role AI played, especially when it did more than assist with grammar, formatting, or organization.

Accountability means a human being remains responsible for the final product. Someone must verify the facts, protect the voice, honor the audience, and stand behind the words.

This is not a rejection of technology. It is a call for editorial discipline.

Every generation of publishing has faced new tools. We have moved from typewriters to word processors, from paste-up boards to digital design, from print-only platforms to websites, social media, video, podcasts, virtual environments, and now AI-assisted content. The tools change. The responsibility remains.

AI is now part of the editorial journey. It is part of the modern writing process. It can be part of the team. But it should never be allowed to become the invisible author of work that claims to carry a human voice.

The future of writing will not be defined by whether we use artificial intelligence. We are already using it. The future will be defined by how honestly, ethically, and intelligently we use it.

For me, the standard is clear. AI may help shape the final presentation, but the purpose must begin with us. AI may strengthen the copy, but the voice must remain ours. AI may support the editorial process, but the responsibility must stay with the human editor, the human writer, and the human institution.

That is how we preserve trust. That is how we protect creativity. That is how we honor the reader.

And that is how AI earns its proper place, not as a replacement for the writer, but as a responsible member of the editorial team.
